opus-5.5.text:
Neural Task Programming was one of my first big projects at Stanford, and honestly it shaped a lot of how I think about research even today.

The core idea was pretty simple to state: robots should be able to learn a new long-horizon task from a single demonstration, the way people can watch someone do something once and get the gist. We framed it as a kind of program induction. The model would take a demonstration and recursively decompose the task into subprograms, down to primitive actions the robot could actually execute. It was inspired by work on neural programmer-interpreters, but we wanted it grounded in real manipulation, things like block stacking and object sorting.

What it taught me, first, is that structure matters. At the time there was a lot of excitement about end-to-end learning, just throw a big network at pixels-to-torques. NTP convinced me that the right inductive biases, like hierarchy and compositionality, can buy you an enormous amount of generalization. A long task isn't one monolithic thing; it's made of reusable pieces. That intuition has stayed with me through almost everything since, from learning task structure to planning with learned models.

Second, I learned to respect the gap between a nice idea and a working robot. In simulation things could look really clean, but once you think about real perception, noisy demonstrations, and failures in the middle of a long task, you realize the hard problems are often not the ones in your paper's title. That pushed me toward caring about robustness and recovery, not just success on a curated benchmark.

Third, it shaped my taste for problems where the question is bigger than the method. The specific architecture in NTP is not what people use today. But the question, how do we get robots to acquire complex, multi-step skills efficiently and generalize them, is still central, maybe even more so now with large models and big robot datasets. I've come to value working on questions that will outlive whatever technique is fashionable that year.

And on a more personal level, it showed me the value of good collaborators and mentors. Working with Fei-Fei and Silvio, and with folks like Yuke Zhu and Animesh Garg, I saw how people with different perspectives, vision, learning, robotics, could come together on one problem. That interdisciplinary flavor is something I try to carry into my own lab now.

r001.rationale: He says Neural Task Programming taught him that structure matters and that hierarchy and compositionality support generalization, indicating a preference for structured research approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Neural Task Programming was really the project that set the tone for how I think about problems. That was back around 2017, 2018, when I was starting my PhD at Stanford with Fei-Fei and Silvio Savarese, and the big question in my head was: how do you get a robot to do something long and structured, like stacking blocks into a particular configuration or sorting objects, when the demonstrations you have are few and the tasks keep changing?

The idea in NTP was to treat a task as a program. You have a demonstration, the network looks at it and decomposes it hierarchically, breaking it into subtasks, then sub-subtasks, until you bottom out in primitive actions the robot can actually execute. What I loved about it, and what I still love, is that the structure was doing the generalization for you. You did not need to see a thousand variations of the task. If the model learned the recursive decomposition, it could compose pieces it had seen into things it had not.

That shaped my taste in a few lasting ways. First, I became a big believer in compositionality and hierarchy as the way to get out of the data trap in robotics. We do not have internet-scale robot data. We probably never will in the same way vision and language do. So you have to ask what inductive biases or what problem decompositions let you get more out of each demonstration. Second, I learned to care a lot about long-horizon problems specifically. A lot of robot learning results at the time were essentially reaching and grasping, and I found that unsatisfying. The interesting failures happen when you have to sequence twenty things and recover when step seven goes wrong.

The third thing is a bit more humbling. NTP worked beautifully in the settings we designed, and it was brittle outside them. The hierarchy was hand-specified in a sense, and that is the tension I have been chasing ever since: how do you keep the benefits of structure without baking in so much that the system cannot adapt? A lot of my later work on learning from play, on task and motion planning with learned components, and now with foundation models, is really still that same question in different clothes. Where should structure come from, and how much of it should be learned?

So if I had to summarize, NTP taught me to value problems with structure, to be skeptical of pure scale as the only answer in robotics, and to pay attention to the gap between a clean demo and a system that actually generalizes. I think that gap is where most of the real research is.

r001.rationale: He says NTP shaped his taste in research and that it taught him to value problems with structure, hierarchy, and compositionality.

astra-6.text:
Working on neural task programming made me interested in the connection between learning and structure. If you want a robot to learn a task from a demonstration, it needs more than a mapping from an image to an action. It needs some way to capture what the steps are, how they fit together, and which parts it can reuse when the situation changes.

That shaped my taste toward problems where learning a skill is only the beginning. The more interesting question is whether you can compose those skills and generalize to a new task. I like research that makes that question concrete—where you can test whether a system learned something reusable, rather than just getting better at the examples it was trained on.

r001.rationale: He says the work sparked his interest in learning and structure and shaped his research taste toward composing skills and testing generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
Neural task programming helped me appreciate the gap between learning a skill and being able to use it as part of a longer task. You can have a system that does individual steps quite well, but composing those steps, knowing when to move on, and recovering when something goes wrong are still really challenging.

That shaped my taste toward problems at the intersection of learning and structure. What should the robot learn from data, and what structure helps it generalize? I became more interested in systems that can reuse what they know across tasks, and in testing those ideas through actual execution. When a robot has to carry out the whole task, you find out very quickly which assumptions hold up.

r001.rationale: The response says neural task programming shaped his research taste toward problems at the intersection of learning and structure, indicating a preference for structured research approaches.
